coverage: Six pre-0 CE Western Amazonia and upper Andean–Amazonian foothill records spanning Late Pleistocene rock shelters, early shellmound ceramics, cacao domestication, earthen forest islands, geometric enclosures, and cliff art.

records.title: Caverna da Pedra Pintada (Monte Alegre, Lower Amazon) — Terminal Pleistocene tropical-forest foragers

location.name: Monte Alegre / Caverna da Pedra Pintada, Pará, Brazil

time.method: AMS radiocarbon and OSL/TL dating of stratified hearth, botanical, and bifacial lithic levels.
time.interpretation: Documents Terminal Pleistocene specialized palm-fruit, fish, and shellfish foraging contemporary with North American Paleoindian traditions.

sources.authors: Anna C. Roosevelt; M. Lima da Costa; C. Lopes Machado; M. Michab; N. Mercier; H. Valladas; et al.
sources.title: Paleoindian Cave Dwellers in the Amazon: The Peopling of the Americas
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

sources.title: (Re)visitando a Amazônia: Serra dos Carajás e Monte Alegre, estado do Pará
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Stratified Triangular-stemmed lithics, ochre pigment droplets, carbonized palm seeds, and painted sandstone walls record tropical-forest occupation by ~11,200–8000 BCE.
claims.explanation: Re-dated botanical, lithic, and sediment samples independently confirm Late Pleistocene–Early Holocene tropical foraging prior to savanna-only dispersal models.

support.note: Primary stratigraphic excavation and multi-method chronology at Pedra Pintada.
Regional comparative reassessment of Monte Alegre and Carajás sequences.

review.summary: Caverna da Pedra Pintada preserves stratified Terminal Pleistocene hearths, carbonized Brazil-nut and palm fruits, bifacial points, and painted panels demonstrating early tropical-rainforest adaptation.
review.limitations: Individual painted motifs above floor deposits remain mostly relative-dated via spalls and ochre associations.
review.discussion: Terminal Pleistocene Amazonian foraging alongside Clovis-age North American traditions.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Caverna da Pedra Pintada, Monte Alegre.

records.title: Taperinha Shellmound (Santarém, Pará) — Early Holocene pottery in riverine Amazonia

location.name: Taperinha, Santarém, Lower Amazon, Brazil
location.provenance: Iriarte et al. (2020) Quaternary Science Reviews 248:106582.

time.method: Thermoluminescence on sand-tempered sherds and radiocarbon dates on freshwater shell.
time.interpretation: Documents some of the earliest known ceramic vessels in the Americas in freshwater sambaqui river-terrace economies.

sources.authors: José Iriarte; Sarah Elliott; S. Yoshi Maezumi; Daiana Alves; Regina Gonda; Mark Robinson; et al.
sources.title: The origins of Amazonian landscapes: Plant cultivation, domestication and the spread of food production in tropical South America
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Freshwater shellmounds at Taperinha yield incised sand- and shell-tempered ceramic bowl fragments dated between c. 6000 and 4000 BCE.
claims.explanation: Syntheses of Early Holocene Amazonian food production corroborate Taperinha's early ceramic sequence alongside incipient cultivation.

support.note: Regional chronological synthesis placing Taperinha in early Amazonian fisher-horticultural sequences.

review.summary: Taperinha preserves thick freshwater mussel middens with low-fired, occasionally incised bowls that predate coastal Andean Formative pottery by millennia.
review.limitations: Reservoir corrections on freshwater shell require cross-checking against charcoal and TL assays.
review.discussion: Independent lowland ceramic invention linked to sedentary floodplain resource harvesting.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Taperinha shellmound.

records.title: Serranía de la Lindosa (Guaviare, Colombian Amazon) — Terminal Pleistocene cliff paintings & hearth floors

location.name: Cerro Azul / Serranía de la Lindosa, Guaviare, Colombia
location.provenance: Morcote-Ríos / Iriarte et al. (2024) Quaternary Science Reviews 328:108522.

time.method: AMS radiocarbon dates on carbonized seeds and ochre-associated hearth strata beneath painted tepui panels.
time.interpretation: Links early northwestern Amazonian colonization across Guaviare forest-savanna margins to monumental ochre rock-art galleries.

sources.authors: Francisco Javier Aceituno; Gaspar Morcote-Ríos; José Iriarte; Mark Robinson; et al.
sources.title: The peopling of Amazonia: Chrono-stratigraphic evidence from Serranía La Lindosa, Colombian Amazon
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

sources.title: Ice Age megafauna rock art in the Colombian Amazon?
sources.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 377:20200496
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Excavated shelters beneath Cerro Azul and Nuevo Tolima walls contain ochre pellets, faunal remains, and palm nuts dated from ~10,500 BCE onward.
claims.explanation: Basal hearth ages around 12.5 ka cal BP are well replicated; specific taxonomic identifications of putative extinct megafauna motifs remain actively debated.

support.note: Chrono-stratigraphic excavation across Serranía La Lindosa rock shelters.
Evaluates zoological interpretations of painted motifs.

review.summary: Serranía de la Lindosa spans kilometers of sandstone overhangs decorated with thousands of hematite pictographs above stratified Late Pleistocene and Holocene occupation floors.
review.limitations: Individual pictographs are mostly indirectly dated through floor ochre nodules and overlapping paint stratigraphy.
review.discussion: Connects Andean-Amazonian piedmont settlement corridors in southern Colombia.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Serranía de la Lindosa, Guaviare.

records.title: Llanos de Moxos Forest Islands (Beni, Bolivia) — Early Holocene cassava, squash & wetland domestication

location.name: Isla del Tesoro & San Francisco Forest Islands, Beni, Bolivia
location.precision: Regional centroid across cored Isla del Tesoro and neighboring forest islands (±15 km).

time.method: AMS radiocarbon and phytolith analyses across anthropogenic shell-and-earth mounds.
time.interpretation: Identifies southwestern Amazonia as an independent Early Holocene center of manioc and squash cultivation inside human-created woodland mounds.

sources.authors: Umberto Lombardo; José Iriarte; Lautaro Hilbert; Javier Ruiz-Pérez; José M. Capriles; Heinz Veit
sources.title: Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Microbotanical phytoliths from over sixty artificial savanna mounds demonstrate manioc (c. 8350 BCE) and squash (c. 8250 BCE) cultivation followed by mid-Holocene maize.
claims.explanation: Geomorphological coring and AMS dating across multiple mounds confirm anthropogenic soil formation and plant domestication.

support.note: Multi-mound phytolith and radiocarbon chronology in Beni.

review.summary: Repeatedly occupied shell and kitchen-midden islands raised seasonally inundated Beni savannas above flood level, creating fertile wooded habitat patches for domesticated crops.
review.limitations: Individual islands aggregate millennia of seasonal accumulation; later Casarabe monumental canals date mainly after 500 CE.
review.discussion: Establishes lowland Bolivia as a primary center of early Holocene plant domestication.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Llanos de Moxos early forest islands.

records.title: Acre Geometric Earthworks (Upper Purus–Abunã, Brazil) — Pre-Common Era ditched ceremonial enclosures

location.name: Fazenda Colorada / Jaco Sá Geoglyphs, Acre, Brazil
location.provenance: Watling et al. (2017) PNAS 114:1868–1873; Saunaluoma / Ranzi.

time.original: c. 1000 BCE–950 CE (early charcoal clearing & ditch construction pre-0 CE)
time.method: AMS radiocarbon dating on embankment soils and charcoal/phytolith paleoecology columns.
time.interpretation: Demonstrates large-scale geometric ditch-and-bank ceremonial architecture within managed bamboo-palm forests before the Common Era.

sources.authors: Jennifer Watling; José Iriarte; Francis E. Mayle; Denise Schaan; Luiz C. R. Pessenda; Neil J. Loader; et al.
sources.title: Impact of pre-Columbian “geoglyph” builders on Amazonian forests
sources.access: Open-access PNAS DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

sources.title: Geography of ancient geometric earthworks and their builders in southwestern Amazonia
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Hundreds of square, circular, and concentric ditched enclosures excavated in Acre date from the first millennium BCE and transformed palm-rich forest composition rather than clearing vast savannas.
claims.explanation: Soil phytoliths, charcoal, and embankment stratigraphy combine to establish managed agroforestry around monumental ditches.

support.note: Paleoecological forest-management evidence around Acre geometric enclosures.
Spatial synthesis of southwestern Amazonian earthwork distributions.

review.summary: Geometrically precise earthen ditches up to several hundred meters across functioned primarily as periodic ceremonial gathering places embedded in enriched palm forests.
review.limitations: Individual enclosures span varying construction episodes from c. 1000 BCE into late pre-Columbian centuries.
review.discussion: Refutes notions of pre-Columbian western Amazonia as untouched wilderness.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Acre geometric earthworks.

records.title: Santa Ana–La Florida (Mayo-Chinchipe, Zamora-Chinchipe, Ecuador) — Early Theobroma cacao domestication

location.name: Palanda / Santa Ana–La Florida, Zamora-Chinchipe, Ecuador
location.provenance: Zarrillo et al. (2018) Nature Ecology & Evolution 2:1879–1888.

time.method: Ancient DNA, theobromine chemistry, and starch-grain residue inside stirrup-spout vessels and stone mortars.
time.interpretation: Provides the earliest secure archaeological evidence of domesticated cacao use on the upper Amazonian slope, alongside Pacific Strombus shell trade.

sources.authors: Sonia Zarrillo; Nilesh Gaikwad; Claire Lanaud; Terry Powis; Christopher Viot; Isabelle Lesur; et al.
sources.title: The use and domestication of Theobroma cacao during the mid-Holocene in the upper Amazon
sources.access: Journal DOI checked via Consensus API 2026-11-23.

claims.text: Ceramic bottles and stone bowls from spiral temple platforms at Santa Ana–La Florida preserve theobromine, cacao DNA, and starch dated back to c. 3500–3300 BCE.
claims.explanation: Independent starch, chemical biomarker, and ancient genomic verification confirm Upper Amazonian cacao domestication 1,500+ years before Mesoamerican attestations.

support.note: Primary multi-proxy biomarker and ancient DNA proof from Palanda vessels.

review.summary: High-rainfall Andean-Amazonian foothill center featuring sunken circular hearths, fine lapidary turquoise/sodalite offerings, Pacific Spondylus shells, and early cacao beverages.
review.limitations: Demonstrates trans-Andean exchange networks earlier than standard highland-only Formative models.
review.discussion: Identifies the Upper Amazon as the cradle of domesticated Theobroma cacao.
review.provenance: Western Amazon early coverage expansion (#35, November 2026).
history: Added sourced record for Santa Ana–La Florida (Mayo-Chinchipe).
